Milestone 2 — Classical ML baseline for skin-lesion classification (MILK10k)¶

Course: Computer Vision and Speech Recognition — EADA Student: Kristof Papp

Code (GitHub): https://github.com/kristofpapp330/milk10k-cv-course/tree/main/notebooks

0. Task and plan¶

Task (project). From the dermoscopic image of a skin lesion, predict Benign vs Malignant (diagnosis_1, with the 123 Indeterminate lesions merged into Malignant = "needs clinical action", as decided in Milestone 1). As an extra, the same pipeline is also run on the 3 original classes (Benign / Malignant / Indeterminate), as in the Session 5 slides.

Why a classical baseline first (Session 5). It tells us (1) whether simple colour and texture signals predict the diagnosis at all, (2) whether the Milestone 1 pipeline works end to end, and (3) gives the number that the CNN of Session 7 must beat.

Plan — the Session 5 baseline recipe

  1. Split: the Milestone 1 lesion-level split (60/20/20 %, grouped by lesion_id, stratified on the 11 classes, seed 42), re-used unchanged. One dermoscopic image per lesion.
  2. Features: handcrafted colour, histogram, texture, GLCM and ABCD-style features, grouped into 5 feature sets.
  3. Models: majority class (the floor), logistic regression, kNN, random forest, SVM (RBF kernel), each with a small hyper-parameter grid.
  4. Model selection on VALIDATION with macro-F1 (accuracy is misleading with ~70 % malignant).
  5. TEST once with the chosen configuration: metrics with 95 % bootstrap intervals, confusion matrix, ROC curve, errors per diagnosis.

How to run: Restart & Run All. The data folder is set in milk10k_pipeline/config.py (or the environment variable MILK10K_DIR). The first run extracts the features from the 5,240 images (about 5–15 minutes) and saves them to outputs/baseline/features_dermoscopic.csv; later runs load that file and take about 2–4 minutes.

2. Features¶

Every image is resized to 256 × 256 and described by 45 numbers in 5 groups (code: milk10k_pipeline/features.py):

group n features idea
colour statistics 6 mean and std of R, G, B overall colour / colour variability (Session 5, Session 2 finding)
colour histograms 24 8 bins × 3 channels, as fractions of the pixels colour distribution (Session 5)
texture 3 edge density (mean Sobel magnitude), roughness (mean 9×9 local variance), Laplacian variance Session 4 filters averaged into one number
GLCM 4 contrast, homogeneity, energy, correlation (32 grey levels, 4 directions) co-occurrence texture (Session 5 "optional extension … good idea for your project")
ABCD 8 asymmetry left-right and top-bottom (2); from a rough lesion mask: area, compactness = perimeter²/(4π·area), share of the image border covered, colour contrast skin − lesion in R, G, B (6) dermatology checklist (Session 5 ABCDE slide)

The 5 feature sets compared: color (30) · texture (3) · color+texture (33) (= the Session 5 vector) · color+texture+GLCM (37) · all incl. ABCD (45).

Correctness check. tests/test_features.py verifies that the code reproduces the hand calculations of the Session 5 slides on the 5×5 toy lesion: histogram [0.36, 0.64, 0, 0], mean 67.6, std 43.2, edge density 279.8.

2.1 What the rough lesion mask sees¶

The ABCD features need a lesion mask. Real segmentation comes in Session 8, so here it is a simple approximation: Gaussian blur (σ = 2) → Otsu threshold → the dark region that overlaps the image centre. The figure shows it on random training images, to judge how reliable these features can be.

In [4]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(config.SEED)
show = pd.concat([train[train["label"] == k].sample(4, random_state=config.SEED) for k in [0, 1]])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(14, 7.4))
for ax, r in zip(axes.flat, show.itertuples()):
    rgb = features.load_for_features(image_paths[r.isic_id])
    mask = features.lesion_mask(features.to_gray(rgb.astype(float)))
    ax.imshow(rgb)
    if mask is not None:
        ax.contour(mask, levels=[0.5], colors="yellow", linewidths=1.5)
    f = feats.loc[r.isic_id]
    ax.set_title(f"{r.dx} ({r.diagnosis_1})\ncompactness {f['mask_compactness']:.2f}, area {f['mask_area']:.2f}",
                 fontsize=9)
    ax.axis("off")
plt.suptitle("Rough lesion mask (yellow) — top row benign, bottom row malignant")
plt.tight_layout(); save("mask_examples"); plt.show()

Observation. The rough mask works on pigmented (brown/black) lesions, but it fails on pale, pink, non-pigmented lesions, which are not darker than the skin: no mask for 695 of 5,240 images (13 %). Their mask features are filled with the train median. The compactness of irregular lesions is high (MEL 3.03, irregular NV 2.48) and that of round ones is about 1 (NV 0.98), as intended.

2.2 Is there ONE feature that separates the classes? (Session 5 question)¶

For each feature alone, the ROC-AUC on the training split (0.5 = useless; values below 0.5 mean the feature is lower for malignant lesions, so |AUC − 0.5| is the strength).

In [5]:
y_tr = train["label"].to_numpy()
F_tr = feats.loc[train.isic_id]
single = pd.DataFrame({"AUC alone": [roc_auc_score(y_tr, F_tr[c].fillna(F_tr[c].median())) for c in feats.columns]},
                      index=feats.columns)
single["strength |AUC-0.5|"] = (single["AUC alone"] - 0.5).abs()
single["higher in"] = np.where(single["AUC alone"] > 0.5, "Malignant", "Benign")
single = single.sort_values("strength |AUC-0.5|", ascending=False)
single.head(12).round(3)

top = single.index[:6]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(18, 3.6))
for ax, col in zip(axes, top):
    data = [feats.loc[train.isic_id[train.label == k], col].dropna() for k in [0, 1]]
    bp = ax.boxplot(data, widths=0.6, showfliers=False, patch_artist=True)
    for patch, cls in zip(bp["boxes"], BINARY):

    ax.set_xticks([1, 2], BINARY); ax.set_title(f"{col}\nAUC alone {single.loc[col, 'AUC alone']:.2f}", fontsize=10)

plt.suptitle("The 6 strongest single features (training split)")
plt.tight_layout(); save("top_features"); plt.show()

Observation. No single feature separates the classes. The best ones reach an AUC of only about 0.70 (|AUC − 0.5| ≈ 0.2). The strongest are the skin–lesion colour contrasts, which are lower in malignant lesions. The reason is the class mix rather than melanoma biology: 67 % of the malignant lesions are BCC, often pink and barely darker than the skin. Most benign lesions are nevi (NV), dark and high-contrast. Malignant lesions also have less round masks (higher compactness) and less blue variability (std_B).

3. Model comparison on VALIDATION (binary task)¶

Every model is a pipeline median imputer → StandardScaler → classifier; the imputer and the scaler are fitted on TRAIN only. class_weight="balanced" is used for logistic regression, random forest and SVM (kNN has no class weights). Hyper-parameter grids (classical.PARAM_GRIDS):

3.1 Best validation macro-F1 for every feature set × model¶

(each cell = the best hyper-parameters of that model on that feature set)

In [9]:
cells = classical.best_per_cell(results)
model_order = list(classical.PARAM_GRIDS)
set_order = list(features.FEATURE_SETS)
grid = cells.pivot(index="feature_set", columns="model", values="macro_f1").loc[set_order, model_order]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.2))
im = ax.imshow(grid.values, cmap="Blues", vmin=grid.values.min() - 0.05, vmax=grid.values.max() + 0.02)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(model_order)), model_order, rotation=20, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(set_order)), set_order)
for i in range(len(set_order)):
    for j in range(len(model_order)):
        v = grid.values[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                color="white" if v > grid.values.mean() + 0.05 else "black")
ax.set_title("Validation macro-F1 (binary) — best hyper-parameters per cell")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.03); plt.tight_layout(); save("val_heatmap"); plt.show()

Observation.

  • Feature sets: colour carries most of the signal (best 0.724). Texture alone is weak (0.595), but adds a little on top of colour (+0.01 with SVM, +0.02 with logistic regression). GLCM helps the linear model (+0.02) but not SVM or random forest. The ABCD features give the best result for every model, with gains of 0.01–0.02.
  • Models: SVM (RBF) ≈ random forest > logistic regression > kNN, for every feature set. The non-linear models gain about 0.015–0.05 over the linear one. kNN is the weakest because all 45 features count equally in its distance, even the useless ones.
  • Every real model is far above the majority floor (0.418).

3.2 The chosen configuration¶

Rule fixed in advance: highest validation macro-F1 (ties: higher balanced accuracy).

In [11]:
best = classical.select_best(results)
print("CHOSEN:", best["feature_set"], "|", best["model"], "|", best["params"])
print(f"validation: macro-F1 {best['macro_f1']:.3f}, balanced acc {best['balanced_acc']:.3f}, "
      f"ROC-AUC {best['roc_auc']:.3f}, sensitivity {best['sensitivity']:.3f}, specificity {best['specificity']:.3f}")

floor = cells[cells["model"] == "majority"].iloc[0]
print(f"majority-class floor: macro-F1 {floor['macro_f1']:.3f}, accuracy {floor['accuracy']:.3f}")

model, cols = classical.fit_config(best, feats, train, "label")
X_va, y_va = feats.loc[val.isic_id, cols].to_numpy(), val["label"].to_numpy()
score_va = classical.scores_of(model, X_va)

CHOSEN: all incl. ABCD (45) | svm_rbf | {'C': 3}
validation: macro-F1 0.741, balanced acc 0.743, ROC-AUC 0.797, sensitivity 0.847, specificity 0.639
majority-class floor: macro-F1 0.418, accuracy 0.718

Observation. The winner is all 45 features + SVM (RBF, C = 3) with a validation macro-F1 of 0.741. The margin over the next configurations is small: random forest 0.739, SVM on the 33 Session 5 features 0.736. With about 1,050 validation lesions, the uncertainty of one score is around ±0.03, so the top 4–5 configurations are practically tied. The selection rule was fixed in advance, so the winner is kept.

3.3 Which features does the chosen model use?¶

Permutation importance on VALIDATION: shuffle one feature at a time and measure how much the validation macro-F1 drops. Works the same way for every model type.

In [12]:
pi = permutation_importance(model, X_va, y_va, scoring="f1_macro", n_repeats=5, random_state=config.SEED, n_jobs=-1)
imp = pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=cols).sort_values(ascending=False)
groups = features.feature_groups(cols)
group_of = {c: g for g, cs in groups.items() for c in cs}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.6))
top15 = imp.head(15)[::-1]
ax.barh(range(len(top15)), top15.values, color="#2a78d6", height=0.7)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(top15)), [f"{c}  [{group_of[c]}]" for c in top15.index], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("drop in validation macro-F1 when the feature is shuffled")
ax.set_title("Top 15 features of the chosen model (permutation importance)")
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout(); save("feature_importance"); plt.show()

print("importance summed per feature group:")
imp.groupby(imp.index.map(group_of)).sum().sort_values(ascending=False).round(4)

importance summed per feature group:
Out[12]:
abcd           0.1670
color_hist     0.0850
texture        0.0403
glcm           0.0395
color_stats    0.0012
dtype: float64

Observation. The model relies most on the ABCD features: the skin–lesion colour contrast (contrast_R/B/G), how much of the image border the lesion covers (mask_border), and asymmetry. Next come GLCM homogeneity and edge density. Colour statistics ≈ 0 does not mean colour is useless: the same information is also in the histograms and the contrasts. Permutation importance gives correlated features low scores, because shuffling one of them leaves its copies intact.

3.4 A clinical operating point (chosen on VALIDATION)¶

The default rule (malignant if the score passes the model's default threshold) weighs both errors the same. A missed cancer is worse than an unnecessary check, so I also fix a second threshold on validation that catches ≥ 90 % of malignant lesions, and report what it costs in specificity.

In [13]:
thr90 = classical.threshold_for_sensitivity(y_va, score_va, target=0.90)
default_pred_va = model.predict(X_va)
if best["sensitivity"] >= 0.90:
    # the default rule already catches >= 90%: keep it (never make the model LESS sensitive)
    thr90 = min(thr90, score_va[default_pred_va == 1].min())
    print("default threshold already reaches >= 90% sensitivity on validation -> it is kept")
pred_va90 = (score_va >= thr90).astype(int)
m90 = classical.binary_metrics(y_va, pred_va90, score_va)
print(f"threshold for >=90% sensitivity (validation): {thr90:.4f}")
pd.DataFrame({"default threshold": {k: best[k] for k in m90}, "sensitivity-90 threshold": m90}).round(3)

4. TEST — evaluated once¶

Everything above (feature set, model, hyper-parameters, threshold) was decided on validation only. The test split is used here for the first and only time, with the chosen configuration trained on TRAIN.

Observation (TEST).

  • macro-F1 0.721 [95 % CI 0.691–0.751] and ROC-AUC 0.803, against 0.417 for the majority class.
  • The drop from validation (0.741) is within the confidence interval. It is the expected small optimism of choosing the best of 105 configurations on validation.
  • At the default threshold the model misses 117 of 751 malignant lesions (16 %) and flags 40 % of benign lesions.
  • The sensitivity-90 threshold reaches 88.3 % sensitivity on test, slightly below the 90 % target because a threshold never transfers exactly to new data. It misses 29 fewer cancers (88 instead of 117) for 11 more false alarms (131 instead of 120).

Observation — the most important finding. The errors are not spread evenly:

  • Melanoma (MEL): only 34 % caught. BCC, AKIEC and SCCKA: about 90 % caught.
  • Benign keratosis (BKL): only 25 % correct. NV: 88 % correct.

The model learned the dominant pattern of the data: dark, high-contrast, pigmented = benign (like NV) and pink, scaly, low-contrast = malignant (like BCC). Melanomas are pigmented, so they look "benign" to it. Benign keratoses are often scaly and irregular, so they look "malignant". The macro-F1 hides this, and clinically it is the worst possible error, because melanoma is the most dangerous of these cancers.

Observation. The missed malignant lesions include pigmented melanomas and very faint pink BCCs. The false alarms are mostly BKL lesions with scales, redness or a yellow crust. Hairs are visible in many images and add edges that have nothing to do with the lesion (Session 5 warning).

It finds 9 of the 23 Indeterminate lesions (39 %). With only 23 such lesions in test this number is very uncertain, and many malignant lesions are also pushed into Indeterminate (64). This supports the Milestone 1 decision to merge Indeterminate into Malignant for the main task.

7. Report¶

7.1 Summary¶

A classical baseline (handcrafted features + scikit-learn models) was developed for the project task, Benign vs Malignant from the dermoscopic image, on the Milestone 1 lesion-level split (3,143 / 1,048 / 1,049 lesions). 5 feature sets × 5 models × small hyper-parameter grids = 105 configurations were compared on validation with macro-F1. The chosen configuration was then evaluated once on test.

validation test test 95 % CI
majority class (floor) — macro-F1 0.418 0.417 —
chosen: all 45 features + SVM (RBF, C = 3) — macro-F1 0.741 0.721 0.691 – 0.751
balanced accuracy 0.743 0.721 0.688 – 0.751
ROC-AUC 0.797 0.803 0.772 – 0.834
sensitivity (malignant caught) 0.847 0.844 0.816 – 0.870
specificity (benign correctly left alone) 0.639 0.597 0.539 – 0.652
sensitivity-90 threshold: sensitivity / specificity 0.900 / 0.581 0.883 / 0.560
3-class extra — macro-F1 (floor 0.273) 0.567 0.518

The baseline number for later milestones: test macro-F1 0.72, ROC-AUC 0.80. The CNN of Session 7 has to beat this, on the same split and with the same metric.

7.2 Discussion¶

  1. The task is learnable from simple signals. Every model clearly beats the majority floor. Colour carries most of the information. The Session 4 texture features help only a little on top of colour, and GLCM only helps the linear model. The dermatology-inspired ABCD features (skin–lesion contrast, border, asymmetry) give the best results.
  2. Model choice matters less than feature choice. SVM ≈ random forest > logistic regression > kNN, but the spread between models (about 0.04) is smaller than between feature sets (up to 0.14). The top configurations are statistically tied on validation.
  3. Honest evaluation. All decisions were made on validation. Test was used once, and its score is close to validation (0.721 vs 0.741, inside the 95 % interval), so the selection overfitted only slightly.
  4. Accuracy would have been misleading. The majority class gets 71.6 % test accuracy and learns nothing; the chosen model reaches only 77.4 % accuracy. Macro-F1 (0.42 → 0.72) and balanced accuracy (0.50 → 0.72) show the real gain.
  5. The model learned the class mix, not malignancy. Because 67 % of malignant lesions are BCC and most benign ones are nevi, it treats pigmented and high-contrast as benign. Consequences on test: only 34 % of melanomas are caught, and 75 % of benign keratoses are called malignant. One overall score hides this. A deployable tool would have to be evaluated per diagnosis, with special attention to melanoma.
  6. Clinical trade-off. Lowering the threshold (fixed on validation) catches more cancers (88 instead of 117 missed) at the cost of a few more false alarms. For a triage tool, where a missed cancer costs more than an extra check, this is the preferable operating point.

7.3 Limitations¶

  • Whole-image features: colour and texture are measured on the whole image, so skin, hairs and the dark dermoscope corners are mixed in with the lesion.
  • Rough mask: the mask is a simple threshold. It fails on 13 % of images (pale, non-pigmented lesions) and sometimes cuts off part of the lesion.
  • Hairs: hairs are strong edges and confuse the texture features (no hair removal was applied).
  • Resizing: every image is resized to 256 × 256, which distorts the aspect ratio. Size features are in pixels, not mm (no scale available).
  • One validation split: selection used a single validation split, not cross-validation, and the top configurations are within the noise of each other.
  • Rare classes: small classes (DF, INF, VASC, BEN_OTH, MAL_OTH and the 3-class Indeterminate) have too few test lesions for reliable per-class numbers.
  • One image per lesion: only the dermoscopic image is used. The clinical close-up and the metadata (age, site) are not used.

7.4 Next steps¶

  • Session 7 — CNN: compare it with this baseline on the same split and metrics, and report recall per diagnosis (especially MEL).
  • Session 8 — segmentation: a proper lesion mask would allow true border, asymmetry and diameter features, and colour measured only inside the lesion.
  • Cheap improvements to the classical model: hair removal (morphological black-hat filter), colour normalisation (colour constancy), and more texture descriptors (LBP, Gabor filters, HSV/Lab colour). Use cross-validation on train + validation for the model selection.
